solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Story detective wants putting on radio

indicators.note: something put on the radio is heard rather than seen, so we want the sound of the word

parts.note: a tail is a detective who follows a suspect

explanation.surface: A detective's story is wanted for a radio broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: To tail someone is to shadow them, so a shadowing detective is a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale is a narrative account, a plain synonym for story.

clue.text: Drink and feel unwell, so they say

indicators.note: what people say is spoken, so the word wanted only sounds like the one clued

parts.note: to ail is to feel unwell

explanation.surface: Drinking leaves you feeling unwell, or so people claim.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale is a kind of beer, so an example of a drink.

clue.text: Chuck out half-cut clergymen in the middle of film

indicators.note: in the middle of says the cut word sits inside the film's title

parts.note: ET is Spielberg's 1982 film about an alien

indicators.note: half-cut says the word loses half its letters, here the back three

parts.note: vicars are Church of England clergymen

explanation.surface: Drunken clergymen are thrown out halfway through a film screening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' (British slang for drunk) trims VICARS to VIC, which goes 'in the middle of' ET.
explanation.definitionFit: To evict a tenant is to throw them out of their home, so it means chuck out.

clue.text: For Spooner, one might put up a hammock and metal fan

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the starts of words, so the opening sounds trade places

parts.note: a hammock is a bed slung between supports
a hanger is something that hangs or puts things up

explanation.surface: A clue about rigging a hammock turns out to describe a heavy metal fan.
explanation.walkthrough: BED HANGER, with the B and H swapped, sounds like HEAD BANGER.
explanation.definitionFit: A headbanger is a fan of heavy metal music who shakes their head violently to the beat.

clue.text: Bag short student digs has grey lining

indicators.note: lining says the next word is put inside the shortened lodgings, like a coat's lining
short says the last letter is cut off

parts.note: halls of residence, or halls, are university student lodgings; digs is British slang for lodgings
the last letter of halls
old means grey, as in grey-haired

explanation.surface: A student carries a bag to cramped lodgings with grey walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' turns HALLS into HALL, and with OLD as its 'lining' it becomes H-OLD-ALL. 'Has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A holdall is a large soft travelling bag that holds everything, so it is a bag.

clue.text: Skate on ice? One wouldn't be suited to that!

definitions.meaning: surface reading: someone gliding on a frozen rink in skates

definitions.text: One wouldn't be suited to that!
definitions.meaning: setter's reading: a skate is a flat fish, and one lying on ice at the fishmonger's is out of its element

explanation.surface: Ice skating is something one person is plainly not cut out for.
explanation.walkthrough: Skate is the flatfish, displayed on ice at the fishmonger's; the idiom for someone uncomfortable in their setting fits it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person ill at ease in unfamiliar surroundings, here applied literally to a dead fish.

clue.text: Mark's black and from Flanders (not the top part)

parts.note: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

indicators.note: not the top part says the first letter is dropped; in a down clue the top is the start

parts.note: Flemish means from Flanders, the Dutch-speaking region of Belgium
the first letter of Flemish

explanation.surface: A painting is described as dark and Flemish, minus its upper section.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the top of a word is its first letter, so 'not the top part' means the opening letter goes; the surface makes it sound like a cropped painting.
explanation.definitionFit: A blemish is a small flaw or spot on a surface, so it is a mark.

clue.text: Longs to have drinks outside with alacrity

parts.note: nips are small shots of spirits; first part

indicators.note: having something outside means being enclosed by it
the second item wraps round the first

parts.note: to pine is to long for
end of NIPS

explanation.surface: Someone yearns to have drinks outdoors, and eagerly.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippiness is quickness or briskness of movement, close in sense to alacrity's speedy readiness.

clue.text: Shrill tart in sleeper, perhaps rounding cape

indicators.note: rounding means going around, so the jewellery's letters close round the headland's letter
in places the pastry inside the jewellery word

parts.note: a sleeper is a small stud earring worn to keep a pierced hole open
a pie is a pastry dish, like a tart
C is the map abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: A pastry tart rides in a sleeping car that swings round a headland.
explanation.walkthrough: A sleeper is not a train berth here but a small stud earring that keeps a fresh piercing open; 'in' and 'rounding' are two separate insertions into that one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An ear-piercing noise is extremely loud and high-pitched, which is what shrill means.

clue.text: Refusal of choppers to waste time over India

indicators.note: throwing away one letter and having another come in its place swaps them

parts.note: choppers are teeth, hence the adjective for teeth
T is the abbreviation for time
India is I in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A dentist refuses to waste time on a trip to India.
explanation.walkthrough: Choppers is slang for teeth, giving DENTAL; its T is thrown out and I takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A denial is a statement refusing or rejecting something, so a refusal.

clue.text: Popular, and formerly saucy, ham

parts.note: in fashion, popular
ex- means former
pert means cheeky

explanation.surface: Describes a ham as a well-liked joint that once had sauce on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' looks like the meat, but is the adjective meaning clumsy, as in ham-fisted or a ham actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham as an adjective means amateurish or clumsy, so it matches inexpert, lacking skill.

clue.text: Fop that dances with Oscar in a pedestrian way

indicators.note: dancing moves around, so the letters get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
Oscar is O in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A dandy dances dully with a man named Oscar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' looks like it means dull, describing the dancing, but it means on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A footpath is a path for people walking, literally a way for pedestrians.

clue.text: More than the standard amount of oil in a pickle?

parts.note: over means more than
oil is measured by the barrel

explanation.surface: Someone holds too much oil and is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The barrel is the standard unit for crude oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Over a barrel is an idiom for being helpless or in difficulty, as is in a pickle.

clue.text: Viewer's complaint: Sir, it isn't entertaining

indicators.note: to entertain is also to hold within, so the phrase contains the word

parts.note: spans the end of Sir, all of it, and the start of isn't

explanation.surface: A TV viewer complains to a knight that something is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewer' suggests a TV watcher, but is the eye, and complaint is an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Iritis is inflammation of the iris, an eye disorder, and the eye is what does the viewing.

clue.text: Humorous release that'll shake a corporation?

definitions.text: Humorous release that'll shake a corporation?

parts.words: Humorous release that'll shake a corporation?
parts.note: surface reading: a funny press release that rocks a big company; setter's reading: corporation is old slang for a paunch, and a hearty laugh makes it wobble

explanation.surface: A comic press statement will shake up a big company.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation is jocular British slang for a large stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep hearty laugh from the gut, the kind that shakes a fat stomach.

clue.text: Get cracking bitter with gents at the King's Head

indicators.note: the gents is placed at, right before, the next piece
with joins the bitter word on, placed after the rest

parts.note: the gents is a men's toilet, and loo is British slang for a toilet

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: sharp and bitter both describe an acid taste

explanation.surface: Drink a bitter beer and use the gents at the King's Head pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The King's Head is a typical British pub name, but here it means K, the first letter of King's.
explanation.definitionFit: Look sharp is a British idiom meaning hurry up, the same urging as get cracking.

clue.text: Win point with a service

parts.note: E is East, a compass point
taken as written
the Royal Navy, one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A tennis player wins a point on serve.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis picture of point and service hides a compass point and the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn is to gain or obtain by effort, so to win.

clue.text: Old man heading for overgrown border of wood

parts.note: one's old man is one's father

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of overgrown

explanation.surface: Father makes for the overgrown edge of a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood' suggests a forest, but a dado is the wooden lower band of a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A dado is a decorative panelled or railed strip along the lower part of a wall, often of timber.

clue.text: Coin scales fashioned in a revivalist style

indicators.note: fashioning something shapes it anew, so the letters are remade

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Coins and scales are made in an old-fashioned style.
explanation.definitionFit: Neoclassic art and architecture revives the forms of ancient Greece and Rome.

clue.text: Not very clear, piercing scream of disbelief!

indicators.note: piercing means going through, so the word for clear goes inside the scream

parts.note: nooo is a drawn-out cry of disbelief
net means clear, as in net profit after deductions

explanation.surface: Someone is not very clear, cut through by a disbelieving scream.
explanation.definitionFit: None too is an idiom for not very, as in none too pleased.

clue.text: Learner with problems missing wide vehicles

parts.note: L is the learner-driver plate

indicators.note: missing something means doing without it, so it is dropped

parts.note: worries are problems
W for wide, the cricket scoring abbreviation

explanation.surface: A learner driver has trouble with wide vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wide vehicles' reads as one phrase but wide is the letter dropped; in cricket a wide is a ball out of the batter's reach.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorries are large goods trucks, so a type of vehicle.

clue.text: Wild about numbers written about Deep Purple?

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: mad means wild

indicators.note: written the other way about, so it runs backwards

parts.note: NOS is the abbreviation for numbers

explanation.surface: A fan goes wild over songs penned about the rock band Deep Purple.
explanation.walkthrough: Deep Purple looks like the British rock band; it is the dark purple colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Damson is a dark plum, and its name is used for the deep purplish colour of the fruit.

clue.text: Machinery dispute that's backed up big cheeses

indicators.note: something backed up has been driven in reverse, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a row is a quarrel
kings are the most important people, big cheeses

explanation.surface: A dispute over machinery has the bosses backing it.
explanation.definitionFit: The workings of something are its internal mechanism or moving parts, its machinery.

clue.text: Russian leader sending up current data, perhaps

indicators.note: current means in fashion, and in a down entry sending it up moves it to the top

parts.note: Vladimir Putin, the Russian president

explanation.surface: The Russian president mocks current data.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' is IN, the last two letters of PUTIN, which move to the top of this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Input is information fed into a computer, and data is one example of it.

clue.text: Winger hit target one time

indicators.note: something hit is knocked about, so the letters end up scattered

parts.note: taken as written
Roman numeral one
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A football winger hits the target once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' looks like a footballer on the flank; here it is anything with wings, a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The great tit is a common garden bird, so a creature with wings.

clue.text: Run through confession of one who won't take The Sun?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pierce with a sharp point

definitions.text: confession of one who won't take The Sun?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: what a person who avoids sunbathing might admit

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Sun' looks like the British tabloid newspaper, but it is sunshine; the answer splits as I'M PALE.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce through with a spike or blade, to run through.

clue.text: Story contrary detective ill-advisedly screens

indicators.note: contrary means going the opposite way, so the letters read backwards
to screen is to shield and hold behind, so the phrase conceals the word

parts.note: the last letter of detective and start of ill

explanation.surface: A contrary detective unwisely shows a story on screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie is an untrue story, as when a child is said to tell stories.

clue.text: Writing supports ribald cops after sacking

indicators.note: a sacking causes upheaval, leaving things thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Written statements back up crude police officers after they are fired.
explanation.definitionFit: Clipboards are boards with a clip holding paper, giving a firm backing to write on.

clue.text: Row about the X-Factor with regressive view

indicators.note: a regressive view looks backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: re means about, concerning
it is that indefinable special quality, the X factor

explanation.surface: A row breaks out over the TV talent show The X Factor and its backward outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: The X Factor is a British TV talent show, but here the phrase means star quality, also called it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is a row or level, as in tiers of seats in a stadium.
